content: The World Health Organization (WHO) emphasizes a public health approach to HIV prevention, treatment, and care, particularly in resource-limited settings. These guidelines provide comprehensive global recommendations on diagnosing HIV infection, managing care for people living with HIV, using antiretroviral (ARV) drugs for both treatment and prevention, delivering services, and monitoring and evaluating programs. This edition updates the 2016 WHO consolidated guidelines on HIV, incorporating new evidence and consolidating relevant guidance published between 2016 and 2021. A key focus of these guidelines is the promotion of a people-centered approach to care. Despite significant progress in improving access to antiretroviral therapy (ART), many populations living with HIV face structural barriers such as stigma, discrimination, criminalization, and violence. These challenges are particularly pronounced for women, young girls, adolescents, and key populations, including men who have sex with men, sex workers, people who inject drugs, individuals in prisons or closed settings, and transgender people. These barriers affect access to care across the HIV care continuum. The guidelines outline essential strategies to create an enabling environment, such as developing supportive norms and policies, working toward decriminalizing behaviors, ensuring financial commitments, and empowering communities. WHO also emphasizes the importance of workforce training to combat stigma, discrimination, and violence, ensuring equitable access to safe and effective healthcare services for all populations. Updated and consolidated guidance for key populations is being developed to strengthen existing clinical and service delivery recommendations, with availability expected in 2022. These consolidated guidelines include all currently valid WHO recommendations, guidance, and good practice statements across the HIV care continuum. Each recommendation references its source guideline. Implementing these recommendations will have significant implications for program prioritization, funding, and service delivery at both national and global levels. The objectives of these guidelines are to provide updated, evidence-based clinical recommendations for a public health approach to ARV drug use for HIV prevention and treatment across all age groups and populations, particularly in settings with limited health system capacity and resources. They also aim to address key operational and service delivery issues to enhance access to HIV prevention, testing, and treatment, strengthen the HIV care continuum, and integrate ARV drug provision into health systems. Additionally, the guidelines provide programmatic guidance for national decision-makers and planners on adapting, prioritizing, implementing, and monitoring these recommendations. The primary audience for these guidelines includes national HIV program managers, but they are also relevant to national advisory boards on HIV treatment and prevention, tuberculosis (TB) and hepatitis program managers, maternal and child health program managers, clinicians, laboratory service managers, people living with HIV, community-based organizations, key population networks, and international agencies providing financial and technical support for HIV programs in resource-limited settings. The development of these guidelines was informed by several guiding principles. Their implementation should contribute to achieving the Sustainable Development Goals and WHO’s Triple Billion targets. The guidelines are based on a public health approach to scaling up ARV drug use along the HIV prevention, treatment, care, and support continuum. They aim to strengthen broader health systems, particularly primary and chronic care, and are informed by local contexts, including HIV epidemiology, resource availability, health system capacity, and cost-effectiveness. Efforts to promote an enabling environment and protect the human rights of people needing HIV services are integral, including ensuring informed consent, preventing stigma and discrimination, addressing criminalizing laws, and promoting gender equity. The guidelines also emphasize the rights and responsibilities of people living with HIV and advocate for their meaningful involvement in decision-making processes. The guidelines were developed through a rigorous process, adhering to WHO’s established procedures. Recommendations are based on the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) approach, which evaluates evidence and formulates recommendations. Systematic reviews and evidence-to-decision frameworks were prepared and presented during guideline development meetings. The guideline development groups included a diverse range of experts, including HIV specialists, researchers, program managers, epidemiologists, human rights experts, and representatives from civil society organizations and networks of people living with HIV. The WHO HIV Civil Society Reference Group advised on the selection of civil society representatives, ensuring appropriate regional and gender representation. To address potential conflicts of interest, all external contributors completed WHO declarations of interest forms. These were reviewed by technical officers, and management plans for declared conflicts were agreed upon and recorded. Conflicts of interest were disclosed at the start of each guideline development meeting, and participation in decision-making was closely monitored. Efforts were made to minimize any potential influence of conflicts of interest. The guidelines were supported by funding from organizations such as the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, the United States President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief, and Unitaid. The guidelines summarize previously published recommendations and compile them into a consolidated framework. The development process involved consultative meetings with experts, health ministries, and communities to identify research questions and priorities. A WHO steering group developed questions for systematic reviews using the PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcomes) format. The GRADE approach was used to appraise evidence and inform discussions during guideline development meetings. External peer review was conducted to ensure the validity, reliability, and clarity of the content. The structure of the guidelines follows the continuum of HIV testing, prevention, treatment, and care. Key chapters address various aspects of HIV care, including testing and diagnosis, prevention, ART for people living with HIV, advanced HIV disease, co-morbidities, service delivery, and monitoring ART program functioning. Each chapter provides detailed recommendations and guidance on specific topics, such as the use of ARV drugs for prevention, rapid ART initiation, managing co-infections and co-morbidities, and integrating HIV services with other health services. The guidelines emphasize person-centered care, reduced clinic visit frequency, community-based approaches to support adherence, and integration of sexual and reproductive health services with HIV care.
